newsitem.title: USA: Heavy Ohio rain seen threat to fledgling crops - WSC.
newsitem.headline: Heavy Ohio rain seen threat to fledgling crops - WSC.

text.p: Heavy rains fell over the weekend in Ohio, posing a possible threat to newly-planted corn and soybean crops, said Joel Burgio, agricultural meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.

"We averaged between 1.5 and 3.0 inches of rain, covering the entire state (of Ohio) and that spilled over into the far southern and southeastern portion of Indiana and also the northern portion of the state of Kentucky," Burgio said.
"There is a possibility with this kind of rain, especially in such a short period of time, you could wash out some of the crop which wasn't firmly established," he said.
Burgio noted that in Findlay, in northwest Ohio, there had been 10.28 inches of rain since May 1, 272 percent of normal.
Further south in Dayton there have been 7.4 inches of rain since May 1, 190 percent of normal.
Weekly state crop reports issued last week indicated Ohio's corn crop was 95 percent planted, as of Sunday May 25, and 57 percent emerged.
The state's soybean crop was 69 percent planted and 20 percent emerged. Crop progress data will be updated later Monday.
"Any remaining planting would be hampered," Burgio said.

Burgio said that during the next 24 to 36 hours there would be further showers in the eastern Corn Belt, although totals would be lower. For western Ohio about 0.25 to 0.50 inches of rain were anticipated.
Showers also fell in Texas and Oklahoma over the weekend although totals were mostly under 0.25 inch and the impact on harvesting of hard red winter wheat was minor, WSC's Burgio said.

"We have pretty favorable conditions for harvesting at least through Wednesday," he said of early efforts to cut winter wheat, noting the outlook for later in the week was uncertain with thunderstorms possible.
